title: Competing studios in New Orleans
summary: Competition was small: radio station recording, National Radio Recording in the Gottschall building, a violin teacher Kilinski with a disc machine, and Johnny Vincent's short-lived studio.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: who was who was your competition in those days if there was anywhere if I came to New Orleans and you were booked I couldn't get I couldn't get your studio

well radio stations did some some of it you know by being almost forced into it I don't think they were looking for it either and didn't want to be bothered with a flock of musicians coming in and not necessarily they wouldn't be bothered after hours but there was a studio in New Orleans national radio recording in the Gottschall building which is no longer here
and I was run by engineer from WWL and Ray McNamara the organist exceptional organist yeah he used to play at the Sanger on that big pipe organ

I was trying to remember the name and I can't recall and then some years later a guy named Kilinski a violin teacher on St. Charles did some recording and mainly he had a little disc machine and mainly for his students but he did things if somebody wanted to come in and record he did recordings but it was mainly for his students you've got to remember the technology was miserable back then you're talking about recording direct to acetate discs and even the finished product wasn't that great if you managed to get a successful record
right so that was that was it that was it

yeah well there were other people who had studios from time to time one time even one of my big customers for a while Johnny Vincent tried to open a studio in town he had a place somewhere in what's now the Warehouse District and I was never there so I don't know it didn't last long a couple other people had studios from time to time some of which were successful but
